claim: The rotary's speed switch decides which of the type's two high-rotor rate bytes the rotor follows, and it turns over between 63 and 64 rather than at the 0x7F the page prints against it. Below that it is the slow byte, at every one of the 8 settings asked there; at and above it the fast byte, at every one of the 5, and the two arms are 0.84 Hz and 9.94 Hz apart so nothing turns on a small difference. With the switch on the fast arm the fast byte moves the rotor over the same printed table the slow byte was closed on -- ten settings, none of them further from an entry than the arrival gap already measured -- and the slow byte stops moving it at all, sitting inside 0.0002 Hz across three settings that span the whole of its range. What the byte does not decide is the arrival: below where the rotor already was, the fast byte lands on its entry to two thousandths of a hertz, and above it the rotor stops short by the same six hundredths the slow byte stops short by. That is the sign the mechanism beside this one predicts -- a lag written as an arithmetic right shift underflows climbing and floors falling -- and nothing here was fitted to it. Both of the readings this left standing were asked and both fell. The turnover is the machine's rather than this type's: the other type that prints the parameter turns over between the same two settings, with the same two rates under it. And the arrival is not the byte's: the same setting of the same byte stops short when it is written a third of a second after the switch and lands on its entry when it is written two seconds after it, which places the rotor between 4.05 and 4.25 Hz at the shorter gap.
named: a two-state parameter decoded from the top bit of its byte, selecting which of two entries of one rate table a rotor is sent to

measurements.read_as: The switch byte swept, which no record had done: every other run of this type holds it and sweeps a rate, so none of them could say what it does at a value the page does not print. The fast byte is parked at the top of its table, so the slow arm reads 0.84 Hz and the fast arm 9.94 and which one the rotor is on is not a judgement about a small difference.

The fast rate byte over the ten settings the slow byte's own law was read on, with the switch at a value that reaches the fast arm. The first reading this byte has ever had: every published sweep of it was taken with the switch below the turnover and returned the slow arm's rate whatever was written.

The slow rate byte under that same block -- the other half of the mirror, and the half that makes it a control. A run that only showed the fast byte moving would not have separated a switch from a byte that came alive; this shows the slow byte going still at the same moment.
The same setting of 40 03 08 after three times the wait. A wait is a parameter, and one wait cannot say it was long enough -- these agree with the ten second takes to a ten-thousandth of a hertz.
The same setting of 40 03 07 after three times the wait. A wait is a parameter, and one wait cannot say it was long enough -- these agree with the ten second takes to a ten-thousandth of a hertz.

Published: the fast byte with the switch at 00. The control this run is read against, and it was already in the archive -- so the only thing that moves between those rows and these is the one byte, and the comparison carries no correction.

Published: the slow byte with the switch unwritten. The control this run is read against, and it was already in the archive -- so the only thing that moves between those rows and these is the one byte, and the comparison carries no correction.

A different two-state parameter, printed 00/01 rather than 00/7F, which answers at 1: a whole filter appears between its two settings, the steepest slope in the profile going from 1.78 to 14.89 dB per octave. It is cited here because it is what stops this claim being read as a rule about two-state parameters -- the page's two spellings are two decodings, and a run that treats either as decoration can get a null with nothing in the record to say the state was never reached.

The store takes every value of this byte and reads it back. That is why the run that wrote it 0x01 got no complaint and no note in its record: what the store accepts is not what the engine reaches, and only a take can tell the two apart.

The same switch byte swept on the other type that prints it, under the block a published record of this type's high rotor was taken with -- the phaser silenced at its own level byte, the low rotor at its own, the rotary and the high rotor at full. The turnover is in the same place, and the two arms are the same two rates this type returns: 0.8374 against 0.8373, and 9.943 against 9.9442.

The first setting on the fast arm asked again after thirty seconds instead of ten. It agrees with the ten second take to three ten thousandths of a hertz, which is what says the shorter wait was past arrival -- one wait says nothing and cannot be checked afterwards.

Four settings four apart across the boundary, with the rate byte written 0.3645 s after the switch -- the gap the published sweep of this address was taken at, reproduced rather than added to. All four stop short, by 0.0588 to 0.0621 Hz. Over the four and not between the ends of them: the largest gap here is not at either end of the settings, so a range read off the first and the last would exclude two of the rows it claims to cover.
The same four with two seconds between the two writes and nothing else changed. All four land on the entry.
The same four again at eight seconds. It agrees with the two second pass to 0.0003 Hz, so the rotor had already arrived by two and the landing is not a longer wait continuing to help.

document_rows.read_as:
The byte values printed against those two states are 0x00 and 0x7F. They are quoted here rather than in the row above because the gate over these citations checks a row's printed setting column and not its byte-value column, so a hex pair put in the row would go unchecked while looking checked. This script reads it out of the file instead and stops if it is not what this says.

That is what makes 0x01 a value with no state printed against it rather than a reasonable spelling of On, and it is the only thing that could have said so: the unit accepts and reads back the whole range. It is not evidence that the engine turns over at 0x40 -- the page says nothing about the 126 values between its two -- which is what the sweep is for.

era_priors.claim: A two-state parameter carried in a seven-bit byte is read by testing its top bit, which is one instruction and no comparison.
era_priors.why: The states the page prints are 0x00 and 0x7F, whose top bits differ, and a machine of this period reading a switch out of a MIDI data byte has a bit test and not a range check to hand.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: The turnover sat anywhere but between 0x3F and 0x40 -- at 0x01, which would be a test against zero, or at 0x7F, which would be a test against the printed state itself. Both were asked and neither is where it is.

adds: Two rate bytes of this type had no reading at all, and the reason was not that the address was wrong. It is that a value the store accepted never reached the state, which nothing in a record can show and only a page can say. What this adds beyond the two bytes is the turnover itself, which is a fact about how this machine decodes a switch and not about a rotary.

what_the_switch_does.why_this_is_a_turnover_and_not_a_curve: Every setting on one side returns one rate to four decimal places and every setting on the other returns the other, with nothing between them at any of the thirteen asked. Two of the thirteen are the settings either side of the turnover, so what is claimed is that it happens at one place and not that it happens somewhere.

what_the_fast_byte_indexes.what_this_is_worth: Nothing was fitted to this byte, so all ten settings were places it could have disagreed. The one it could not answer is the bottom of the byte: the table puts setting 0 at 0.05 Hz and an eight second take cannot carry two cycles of anything under 0.301, so that row is the take's floor and is published as a null rather than as a rate.

which_way_the_rotor_was_sent.what_separates_the_two_groups: Where the rotor already was when the byte arrived. The settings that land on their entry are the ones below it and the ones that stop short are above it. Round one placed the boundary between the settings whose entries are 4.05 and 4.85 Hz, which is as close as the sweep's own grid could put it; round two asked four settings inside that span and puts it between 4.05 and 4.25.
which_way_the_rotor_was_sent.why_it_is_not_the_byte_s_own_default: The page prints this byte's default at 7.50 Hz, which is setting 120, and three settings below that stop short. So whatever the boundary is, it is not the byte powering up somewhere -- which is what it is on the slow byte, where the boundary is that byte's own printed default to the setting.
which_way_the_rotor_was_sent.what_this_run_cannot_say: Round one could not say where the boundary was, closer than the 0.8 Hz between the two settings that straddled it, because the gap between the two writes was never varied. It has been: the reading is under `where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrived`, which places the rotor between 4.05 and 4.25 Hz and shows the boundary moving with the gap. What is still not read is how fast the rotor climbs, which two bounding points do not shape and which the acceleration byte's own claim is the place for.

and_the_other_spelling_of_a_two_state_pa: This unit prints 58 two-state parameters and spells them two ways: four as 00/7F, all four of them a rotary's speed switch, and 54 as 00/01. The second spelling does not behave like the first. One of them has a sweep in this archive -- the amp switch of 01 10 -- and a whole filter appears between its 0 and its 1: the profile's largest band goes from 3.98 dB to -19.24 and its steepest slope from 1.78 dB per octave to 14.89. So that one is reached at 1 and does not wait for the top bit. Which rule it does follow is not read here and would need its own sweep. What is established is that the spelling is not decoration, and a run that writes a two-state byte without reading which spelling it has can get a null with nothing in the record to say the state was never reached.

alternatives.reading: The boundary between landing on the entry and stopping short is a property of the byte or of the table rather than of where the rotor was when the byte arrived.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It was asked, and one byte at one setting returns two rates. Written 0.3645 s after the switch, all four settings across the boundary stop short by about six hundredths of a hertz; written two seconds after it, all four land on their entry, and at eight seconds they agree with the two second pass to two ten thousandths. A property of the byte or of the table cannot move with when the byte was written, and this one moves the whole way -- from every setting short to every setting landing -- on a change that touches nothing but the gap.

alternatives.reading: The turnover is a test of the top bit rather than a comparison against 64, or against the halfway point of the printed range.

separated_by.observable: Nothing a seven-bit byte can carry.

predicts.the top bit: slow below 64 and fast at and above it

separated_by.sensitivity_here: Not applicable. Over the values this byte has, the top bit being set and the value being at least 64 are the same condition, so the two readings agree at all 128.
separated_by.why_not_separable: They differ in which instruction the part runs and in nothing that comes out of the sockets. The claim does not rest on the difference: what it states is where the turnover is, and both readings put it there.

alternatives.reading: The other three types that print this parameter decode it some other way, so the turnover is this type's and not the machine's.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: It was asked on one of them. `11 07` prints a rotary beside a phaser and its switch at a different address, and it turns over between 63 and 64 as well: four settings below return 0.8374 Hz and four at and above return 9.9429 to 9.9432. The other two types are not asked, so what this rules out is the reading that the turnover is one type's -- a second type deciding it the same way is not two types deciding it differently.

refuted_by: A take at a setting below 64 that returns the fast byte's rate, or one at or above it that returns the slow byte's. Either would mean the turnover is not where this puts it, and each of the thirteen settings asked was a place that could have happened. Also by the fast byte returning something that is not the printed table: it was read at ten settings and no entry was fitted, so any of the ten could have refused.
what_this_does_not_settle: What the low rotor's fast byte does. The page prints that rotor's acceleration at 3 of 0-15, near the bottom, and the claim beside this one measured a rotor still climbing at ten seconds and at forty-five down there. So it needs a wait this run's ten seconds is not, and asking it under this run's wait would return a ramp's average and look like a rate.
Which rule the 54 parameters printed 00/01 follow. One of them is measured to answer at 1, which is enough to say the two spellings are two decodings and not enough to say what the second one tests.

Whether every setting of the switch on the slow side is the slow byte or only the eight asked. The eight span the side and include both ends of it, and the byte is read by one test under every reading here, but the 120 not asked are not asked.

Whether the other two types that print this parameter turn over there too. One of the three was asked and does; the two that were not are 11 08 and 11 09, and the archive already reads a multi as reaching a single type's block, which makes one rule the thing to expect rather than the thing to assume.

where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrive.what_was_varied: The gap between writing the speed switch and writing the rate byte, and nothing else. The held block, the note, the ten second wait after the rate byte and the four settings are the same in all three passes.
where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrive.what_it_says: One byte at one setting returns two rates, and which one it returns depends only on when it was written. So the arrival is not a property of the byte or of the table entry: it is a property of where the rotor already was, which is what the lag beside this claim says and what this run was made to test.
where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrive.where_the_rotor_was: Between 4.05 and 4.25 Hz, 0.3645 s after the switch was written. The published sweep lands on the entry at setting 80, whose entry is 4.05, so the rotor was at or above it; this run stops short at setting 84, whose entry is 4.25, so the rotor was below that. Round one could only say the rotor was somewhere between 4.05 and 4.85, and the two settings it had there were 0.8 Hz apart.
where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrive.how_the_gap_itself_is_known: Timed rather than read off the sleep in the source. The preparation writes an address, sleeps 0.350 s and reads it back, and the readback is a round trip to the unit that nothing in the source states: measured ten times it is 0.0145 s, for 0.3645 s between the two writes, 0.3607 to 0.3652 across the ten. Untimed, the shortest pass is a gap of at least a third of a second and the rate above is a bound with one side open.
where_the_rotor_was_when_the_byte_arrive.what_is_still_not_read_here: How fast the rotor climbs. Two points on one climb -- at rest when the switch is written and between 4.05 and 4.25 a third of a second later, arrived by two seconds -- bound it and do not shape it, and the byte that sets it has its own claim beside this one. What this adds there is a figure that claim can be held against, not a fit made here.

the_turnover_is_the_machines_and_not_thi.asked_on: 11 07, which prints a rotary beside a phaser and a switch at 40 03 11 rather than 40 03 0D
the_turnover_is_the_machines_and_not_thi.what_it_says: The turnover is between 63 and 64 on this type too, so it is the machine's rule for a two-state parameter printed 00/7F and not one type's implementation. Round one could not say which: one type's switch turning over at the top bit is one type's switch.
the_turnover_is_the_machines_and_not_thi.and_the_two_types_return_the_same_rates: The slow arm reads 0.8374 here against 0.8373 there and the fast arm 9.943 against 9.9442, under held blocks that silence the same things. That is the shared table showing up across two types, which is a separate claim's and is cited here rather than made.
the_turnover_is_the_machines_and_not_thi.why_the_phaser_had_to_be_silenced: This type prints two modulators and a take returns whichever dominates it, so a rate read with the other stage audible is not evidence about this byte. The block is copied from the published record that established that here: the same slot with only the phaser turned down returns 6.4202 Hz at a setting where the fully silenced block returns 1.5886.
